strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap: the lack of a standardized, unified benchmark for video-based fall detection, which has been fragmented across many small, incompatible datasets.
The systematic, PRISMA-guided dataset collection and inclusion/exclusion criteria are transparently documented, giving credibility to the curation process.

Re-annotating eight existing datasets under a consistent ten-class taxonomy that distinguishes transient actions (fall, sit down, lie down, stand up) from sustained states (fallen, sitting, lying, standing) is a meaningful and clinically well-motivated contribution, since detecting the sustained 'fallen' state (long-lie) is what matters for mortality.

Introducing OOPS-Fall from genuine accident videos and defining a staged-to-wild evaluation protocol is a useful step toward measuring real-world generalization rather than only in-distribution performance.
The benchmark provides cross-subject and cross-view splits, plus domain-shift analysis via FVD and T-SNE/H-NNE visualizations, which help characterize the domain gap concretely.
Limitations and societal impact are discussed thoughtfully (surveillance/privacy, false alarms, demographic bias, human oversight), which strengthens the work's framing.
Resources (OmniFall and code) are promised for release, supporting reproducibility and community use.
weaknesses: The core contribution is essentially re-annotation and re-organization of existing public datasets; there is no new algorithm or methodological innovation. While acceptable for a benchmark paper, the scientific insight beyond 'a domain gap exists' is limited.

Experimental evaluation is thin: only frozen backbones (I3D, VideoMAE) are tested, with no fine-tuning of full models and no comparison against existing fall-detection methods, so it is unclear whether OmniFall enables meaningful head-to-head benchmarking.

Key methodological details are missing: how original annotations were mapped to the new ten-class taxonomy, the annotation protocol for OOPS-Fall (number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, adjudication), and how class boundaries (e.g., 'sitting' vs. 'lying' vs. 'fallen') were disambiguated across datasets.

The in-the-wild test set (OOPS-Fall, ~1.3k segments from a single source) is small and drawn from one dataset, so the staged-to-wild conclusions rest on limited evidence; generality of the robustness claims is not established.
The claim of establishing 'the first rigorous staged-to-wild evaluation protocol' is somewhat overstated given the narrow test set and lack of comparison to prior evaluation protocols.
Several important results (e.g., VMAE-K400-Pre) are relegated to supplementary material, making the main paper harder to assess and reducing the visibility of a key backbone comparison.

Interpretations of backbone behavior (e.g., I3D's 'simpler feature space capturing fundamental motion patterns') are speculative and not directly validated; frozen-feature conclusions may not transfer to fine-tuned settings.

Some numbers are not fully reconciled (e.g., abstract reports 29 camera views while Table 1 sums to 31 across datasets), and the total duration accounting across recordings vs. views could be clearer.
No analysis of whether the ten-class taxonomy is clinically validated or whether the balanced-accuracy/F1 metrics used correspond to operationally meaningful thresholds for deployment.

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear clinical relevance: the paper correctly emphasizes that detecting the *sustained fallen state* (rather than only the transient fall event) is what matters for preventing long-lie mortality, and it frames the contribution around this gap.

Genuinely useful benchmark contribution: unifying eight public fall datasets under a single consistent ten-class taxonomy (distinguishing transient actions from static states) directly addresses the annotation-incompatibility problem that has prevented cross-dataset comparison in this field. Table 1 and Figure 3 document this carefully.

Systematic, PRISMA-guided dataset collection and inclusion/exclusion criteria (including transparent reasons for excluding UR Fall, MUVIM, FPDS, etc.) make the dataset curation auditable and reproducible in principle.

The staged-to-wild evaluation protocol using OOPS-Fall is a conceptually valuable addition: it moves the field beyond single-environment evaluation and quantifies the controlled-to-uncontrolled domain gap, which is exactly where deployment matters.
Defined cross-subject and cross-view splits per dataset are a meaningful methodological contribution that supports fair and multi-faceted evaluation.

Domain-shift analysis is informative: the pairwise FVD heatmaps (Figure 4) and t-SNE/H-NNE visualizations (Figure 5) concretely support the claim of large domain gaps and are a nice diagnostic addition to a benchmark paper.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, and it includes an honest Limitations section (demographic bias, limited wild coverage, privacy concerns) plus a thoughtful Societal Impact discussion.

Comparison across three frozen backbones (I3D, VideoMAE-Base, VideoMAE-K400) yields an interesting and non-trivial observation that a coarser ImageNet/Kinetics-supervised representation generalizes better to in-the-wild binary fall detection, which is worth reporting.
weaknesses: The re-annotation of all eight staged datasets under the new ten-class taxonomy is the central claim, yet the main paper provides no details on the annotation procedure: who annotated, what guidelines were used, how ambiguous boundaries (e.g., lie down vs. fall vs. fallen) were resolved, whether inter-annotator agreement was measured, or how quality was controlled. For a benchmark paper this is a critical omission that undermines confidence in the labels.

OOPS-Fall curation is under-described. The paper states it filtered ~1.3k fall/no-fall segments and manually verified them, but does not report how many genuine falls remain, the annotation protocol, or how representative this single wild set is of real-world falls. A single, non-fall-native test source is a thin basis for broad generalization claims.

No comparison against existing fall detection methods or fine-tuned baselines. Only frozen backbones with a lightweight temporal transformer are evaluated, so the benchmark lacks reference points that would let the community situate new methods. This limits the immediate utility of the benchmark.

Several key takeaways are either expected or speculative. The in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution gap is unsurprising, and the explanation for I3D's robustness ('simpler feature space may capture more fundamental motion patterns') is asserted rather than tested; no probing experiment substantiates this mechanism.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the 'OmniFall' and 'Code' links are placeholders, and there is no statement about licensing, consent, or release terms for the re-annotated benchmark, which is essential for a dataset contribution.

The taxonomy does not address temporal boundary handling for transitions (e.g., how the fall-to-fallen transition is segmented and scored), which directly affects the reliability of the segmentation and classification metrics reported.

The claim of establishing 'the first rigorous staged-to-wild evaluation protocol for fall detection' is strong and is not substantiated against prior cross-domain/transfer fall detection work; a more careful positioning would strengthen the paper.

Some results are hard to interpret from the main text alone (e.g., the very large sensitivity gap between I3D and VideoMAE-K400 on OOPS-Fall), and no ablation isolates whether this stems from the backbone, the classifier, or the training-data composition.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and under-served application (fall detection and, crucially, the sustained 'fallen' state) with a clear medical motivation, and correctly identifies three real limitations of prior work: event-only detection, poor cross-environment generalization, and the absence of a standardized benchmark.

The dataset consolidation effort is systematic: a PRISMA-style search with documented inclusion/exclusion criteria, a transparent Table 1 characterizing the eight constituent datasets, and explicit justification for excluded datasets (UR Fall, MUVIM, FPDS, etc.). This is the kind of curation work the community needs.

The proposed ten-class taxonomy that explicitly separates transient actions (fall, sit down, lie down, stand up) from static states (fallen, sitting, lying, standing) is a sensible design choice that enables both event detection and fallen-state detection, and the per-dataset cross-subject and cross-view splits (following original protocols where available) are a meaningful step toward comparable cross-dataset evaluation.

The staged-to-wild protocol built on OOPS-Fall, curated from genuine accident videos, is a rare and valuable evaluation design in this domain; most prior work evaluates only in-distribution on staged data.

The domain-shift diagnostics (pairwise FVD heatmaps across I3D/VideoMAE variants, plus T-SNE and H-NNE embeddings in Figure 5) are useful and directly support the central claim that dataset identity, not activity class, dominates the feature space.
The finding that a frozen I3D generalizes to OOPS-Fall better than a Kinetics-fine-tuned VideoMAE (which overfits and collapses to near-zero sensitivity) is non-obvious and worth reporting.
Limitations (demographic bias toward young subjects in controlled settings, partial coverage of real-world scenarios, privacy) and societal impact are explicitly discussed rather than omitted.
weaknesses: The re-annotation of eight datasets under a unified taxonomy is the paper's core asset, yet the annotation process is completely undocumented: no annotator information, no annotation protocol, no inter-annotator agreement, no quality control, and no statistics on how labels were transferred or corrected. The taxonomy's fragile boundaries (fall vs. sit down vs. lie down; fallen vs. lying) are exactly where such a unification is most error-prone, so the central 'consistent taxonomy' claim is unverifiable. For a benchmark paper this is a fundamental omission.

OOPS-Fall carries only binary fall/non-fall labels, so the headline ten-class taxonomy cannot be evaluated out-of-distribution at all. Tables 2 and 3 leave the ten-class OOD columns blank, meaning the advertised staged-to-wild protocol tests a substantially weaker task than the paper claims. The two pillars of the contribution (fine-grained unified taxonomy, in-the-wild evaluation) do not actually connect.

The OOPS-Fall curation is underspecified: the number of fall vs. non-fall segments, how non-fall segments were sampled (random vs. hard negatives), how clip-level OOPS tags were converted into segment-level labels, and what selection biases this introduces. Without this, the OOD numbers are hard to interpret or reproduce.

The baselines are weak and unrepresentative of the field. Only frozen pre-trained features plus a small temporal transformer are evaluated; there is no fine-tuned or end-to-end baseline, and no pose/skeleton-based baseline even though several constituent datasets (CMDFall, UP Fall, EDF, OCCU) provide skeleton or depth data and pose-based methods dominate the fall-detection literature. As a result the benchmark does not establish achievable performance or connect to the dominant methodology.

Handling of dataset heterogeneity is under-described. Frame rates vary from 18 to 30 fps and resolutions from 320x240 to 1280x720; the paper never explains clip construction (length, stride), temporal resampling, or how conflicting label semantics across datasets are reconciled when merging into one training pool. The dataset-balancing weight with an arbitrary cap of 20 is introduced without any ablation.

No variance or seed reporting anywhere; all results appear to be single runs. It is also unclear whether the 'Overall' rows are macro- or sample-weighted averages, and Tables 2-3 contain missing cells and inconsistent bolding, which makes the reported comparisons harder to trust.

Internal inconsistencies: Section 4.3 states MS-TCN++ is trained 'excluding OOPS-Fall for out-of-distribution testing,' yet Table 4 reports an OOPS-Fall row; how ten-class segmentation outputs were mapped onto OOPS-Fall's binary labels to compute F1@IoU is never explained. Similarly, the text claims I3D 'is the only model that maintains high binary fall detection sensitivity' while VMAE-K400's specificity is 0.97 with sensitivity 0.21, i.e., near-degenerate; this is a weak quantitative basis for the framing of the take-aways.

The clinical framing (long-lie episodes, prompt intervention) is not matched by the evaluation. There are no time-to-detection, sustained-fallen-duration, or false-alarm-rate-over-time metrics; classifying a 'fallen' class within a clip does not demonstrate long-lie monitoring, which is the motivating problem.

Related work is thin (roughly half a page) and restricted to datasets, omitting the broader fall-detection literature (pose-based, transformer-based, multimodal, and prior survey/benchmark efforts). This weakens the positioning and makes the 'first rigorous staged-to-wild evaluation protocol' claim hard to substantiate.

Reproducibility and attribution gaps: the OmniFall and Code links are empty placeholders, and several references have incomplete or malformed entries (missing years/venues for [3], [6], [10], [14], [15], [17], [24]), which does not inspire confidence in the care taken. There is also no discussion of licensing or consent for re-annotating and redistributing human video.

No evidence that the unified benchmark reveals anything prior single-dataset protocols could not. The conclusion that domain gaps exist is expected, and there is no head-to-head comparison against a simpler protocol, no leakage/overlap analysis (some constituent datasets originate from the same groups and environments, e.g., EDF/OCCU), and no demonstration that cross-dataset training actually changes conclusions about which models are preferable.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and under-served problem (fall detection with emphasis on the sustained *fallen* state rather than only brief fall events), with clear motivation grounded in real medical statistics.

Substantial and well-documented dataset/benchmark contribution: aggregation of eight public staged datasets into a harmonized 16-class frame-level taxonomy, with dataset-specific cross-subject and cross-view splits, is a meaningful standardization effort that enables cross-dataset comparison that was previously impossible.

The synthetic data component (OF-Synthetic) with explicitly controlled demographic and environmental diversity (age, ethnicity/skin tone, BMI, environment, camera) is a novel and privacy-amenable contribution that directly targets documented bias in existing staged corpora.
A standardized staged/synthetic -> wild (OF-In-the-Wild) evaluation protocol is provided, including a curated test-only wild split, which is a useful and reproducible benchmark design.

The paper is clearly written, with an unusually thorough appendix covering annotation software/tooling, annotation-team training, QA protocol, PRISMA-informed dataset search, prompt construction, safety filtering, and feature-extraction configurations, which supports reproducibility and appropriate attribution of sources.
Limitations and societal impact are candidly discussed (representativeness of OF-ItW, generator-induced biases, surveillance/privacy concerns), which strengthens rather than weakens the assessment.

The empirical finding that controlled synthetic data can match or modestly surpass real staged data for out-of-distribution generalization, and that appearance-centric (SigLIP2) vs motion-centric (I3D) features benefit differently from synthetic vs staged data, is an interesting and actionable observation for the community.
weaknesses: The headline empirical claim (synthetic data can match/surpass real staged data for cross-domain transfer) rests on relatively small margins on a small, atypical test set. For example, OF-Syn alone reaches 64.2% Fall F1 on OF-ItW vs. 60.5-61.2% for OF-Staged, and combined training adds only ~+1.4 F1 points; without significance testing or additional backbones these differences are not strongly established.

OF-In-the-Wild is only 2.6h / 818 videos / ~1.3k segments curated from OOPS, which consists largely of web/sports/stunt videos rather than genuine elderly falls in care environments. The paper's central 'in-the-wild' claim therefore has representativeness concerns, and generalization conclusions drawn on this split may not transfer to the deployment setting the paper motivates.

Experimental evidence is methodologically thin for a benchmark paper: classification is evaluated with a single frozen backbone (VideoMAE-K400) plus a light transformer head, and timeline segmentation with a single method (ASQuery) using frozen I3D/SigLIP2 features. No comparison to recent state-of-the-art fall-detection or action-segmentation methods is provided, so the benchmark's discriminative power and difficulty are not fully characterized.

The validity of diffusion-generated (Wan 2.2) fall videos as a proxy for real falls is not deeply validated. The authors note the model's tendency to generate smiling faces and other artifacts, which raises the concern that models may exploit spurious appearance cues rather than fall biomechanics; this is not directly tested (e.g., no per-clip human verification of physical plausibility beyond safety filtering).

The domain-shift analysis relies heavily on FVD, t-SNE, and H-NNE, which are known to be imperfect and sometimes misleading proxies for transferability; the claim that OF-Syn is 'closer' to OF-ItW in feature space is used to support the synthetic-data conclusion but is not corroborated by an independent transfer metric.

No code, model weights, or dataset are available for review (released 'upon acceptance'), and some splits are only summarized in the appendix, limiting the ability to independently verify the reported results at review time.

The taxonomy collapses several datasets into a shared 16-class space (e.g., CaucaFall single-view participates only in training for cross-view evaluation), and it is not fully clear how much label noise or ambiguity is introduced by forced harmonization across heterogeneous sources.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: robust fall detection and sustained fallen-state recognition under real-world domain shift, with privacy-aware data collection.

OmniFall is a substantial, well-organized benchmark: it unifies eight staged fall datasets under a harmonized 16-class frame-level taxonomy, provides cross-subject/cross-view splits, and releases dense timeline annotations.

The OF-In-the-Wild component is a valuable test-only benchmark curated from genuine accident videos (OOPS), manually verified and annotated, enabling staged/synthetic-to-wild OOD evaluation that prior fall datasets lack.

OF-Synthetic contributes controlled demographic and environmental diversity via structured prompts and deterministic attribute assignment; the privacy-preserving synthetic data can be shared more easily than sensitive fall footage.

The domain-shift analysis is thorough: FVD heatmaps and t-SNE/H-NNE visualizations across I3D, VideoMAE-K400, and SigLIP2 support the claim that synthetic data lies closer to wild data in feature space.

The experiments, while limited, cover both action/fall classification and timeline segmentation, compare multiple training sources, and show that data diversity rather than only quantity improves cross-domain generalization.

Reproducibility is strong: the appendix documents annotation workflow, PRISMA search, source licenses, splits, feature extraction settings, and generation prompts; limitations and societal impact are discussed.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the main contribution is dataset aggregation, annotation standardization, and synthetic data generation rather than a new algorithm. This is acceptable for a benchmark paper but should be evaluated as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General.

The synthetic data is generated by a single model (Wan 2.2) and is not validated perceptually or with human studies for realism; claims that synthetic data can match or surpass real staged data may be generator-specific and may not transfer to other generators or clinical fall scenarios.

OF-Synthetic has low temporal complexity (compact fall events; median 2 segments versus 116 for CMDFall), which may under-support the sustained fallen-state detection that the introduction emphasizes; this mismatch should be analyzed more directly.

Evaluation is narrow: one classification backbone (VideoMAE-K400) and one segmentation model (ASQuery) are used, without fall-specific baselines, recent video foundation models, or domain-adaptation methods. This weakens the evidence for broad robustness.

OF-ItW is small (2.6 h, 818 videos) and derived from OOPS; it may not represent the full diversity of real falls (e.g., nighttime, severe occlusion, care-home settings). Cross-attribute generalization is only tested on synthetic data, not on real wild data.
The annotation harmonization lacks inter-annotator agreement metrics or adjudication statistics; consistency across eight source datasets remains difficult to verify.

Release and reproducibility may be constrained by source-dataset licenses (some require explicit permission), and the paper's '80 hours / 15k videos' count includes multi-view duplicates, which could be clarified to avoid overstating single-view data size.

strengths: Substantial annotation and engineering effort: harmonizing eight heterogeneous staged fall datasets under a single 16-class frame-level taxonomy, with dataset-specific cross-subject and cross-view splits, is a genuine and non-trivial benchmark contribution that addresses a real problem (annotation heterogeneity preventing cross-dataset comparison).

Well-motivated problem framing and protocol: the staged/synthetic → wild cross-domain evaluation isolates a practically important generalization gap that prior fall-detection datasets do not measure, and the inclusion of a timeline-segmentation task alongside classification is useful.

The synthetic component (OF-Syn) is thoughtfully designed with explicit, documented factorial control over age, ethnicity/skin tone, BMI, clothing, environment, and camera parameters, and the deterministic attribute assignment aids reproducibility. The ethical rationale (privacy-preserving alternative to collecting data from vulnerable elderly populations) is sound and clearly argued.

Good scholarly hygiene: a PRISMA-style systematic dataset search, explicit license/attribution table for source datasets, an appendix detailing annotation tooling, splits, feature extraction, and quality control, plus a limitations and societal-impact section.

The empirical observation that appearance-centric features (SigLIP2) benefit from synthetic diversity while motion-centric features (I3D) benefit from staged data is a potentially useful insight for future benchmark users.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim—that synthetic data can match or surpass real staged data for staged→wild transfer—rests on a single, very small held-out test set (OF-ItW, only 2.65 h / 818 videos derived from OOPS). The reported margins (e.g., OF-Syn Fall F1 64.2% vs. 60.5–61.2% for staged data) are small, and no confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests are provided, so the claim is not adequately supported.

The finding that OF-Syn and OF-ItW are the two most similar domains in feature space (FVD/ t-SNE/ H-NNE, Fig. 4–5) is presented as supporting evidence but could equally indicate that the synthetic training distribution happens to match the specific test set's idiosyncrasies (both are non-staged, both likely share generator/YouTube-like artifacts). This confound is not addressed, and the 'synthetic beats real' conclusion may therefore be partly an artifact of test-set construction rather than genuine generalization.

The synthetic data lack the temporal structure the task requires: the authors' own analysis (Appendix) shows OF-Syn contains almost no full fall→on_floor→stand_up chains (25.0%/0.0% vs. 100%/100% for CMDFall) and 'tightly centers the discriminative fall window.' This directly undercuts claims that synthetic video is a viable substitute for real staged data for sustained-fallen-state detection, which the paper itself motivates as the critical capability.

The demographic-generalization results (cross-age, cross-BMI, cross-ethnicity) are evaluated only within the synthetic domain (Fig. 7). Because the synthetic set was generated with controlled demographic attributes, these splits are largely circular and do not demonstrate that the added demographic diversity improves real-world generalization—the very motivation for the synthetic component.

Experimental validation is thin for a benchmark paper: a single classification backbone (VMAE-K400) with a lightweight transformer head and a single segmentation model (ASQuery). No baselines spanning the range of methods the benchmark is meant to serve, and no error bars or ablations isolating the effect of the taxonomy granularity (e.g., 16-class vs. binary fall/fallen).

The 16-class taxonomy appears over-engineered relative to the task: macro-F1 values are very low (often 30–50) across all configurations, and several classes (squat_down, kneel_down, crawl, sit_down, etc.) are hard to distinguish and only loosely relevant to fall detection. It is not shown that the fine-grained taxonomy is learnable or practically useful rather than an artificial difficulty multiplier.

The necessity of the full unified benchmark is not established: combined OF-Staged+OF-Syn training improves over OF-Syn alone by only ~1.4 F1 points, which weakens the case that the staged aggregation and the unified cross-domain protocol are required rather than the synthetic component alone.

Reproducibility is currently limited: the datasets and code are only promised 'upon acceptance,' and the OF-ItW curation (how 818 fall clips were filtered from OOPS tags and manually verified, and how many were rejected) is not described in enough detail to assess selection bias or to reproduce the test set.

Minor but pervasive presentation issues (inconsistent dataset naming such as OF-ItW / OF-In-the-Wild, figure/table cross-references, and radar-plot color coding) reduce clarity, and several appendix figures (Figs. 9–20) are unlabeled scatter plots of limited interpretive value.
